options: A program in execution, with its own memory, registers and state
Any file that has execute permission
questions.explain: A program is a passive file; a process is that program running. The same program can be running as several processes at once, each independent of the others.

questions.prompt: Which of these is NOT kept in the process control block (PCB)?
options: The pid and the parent's pid
The saved values of the CPU registers
The C source code the program was compiled from
questions.explain: The PCB holds what the system needs to manage the process: identifiers, state, saved registers and program counter, accounting and scheduling data, memory tables and open files. The source code is not part of a process at all.

questions.prompt: Put the life of a typical process in order.
items: Ready: it waits for a CPU
Waiting: it asks for disk I/O
questions.explain: A process is admitted to the ready queue, runs until it asks for I/O (then waits), goes back to ready when the I/O completes, and so on until it exits. It never goes from waiting straight to running.

questions.prompt: Match each state change with its cause.
pairs: it asks for I/O or waits for an event
the I/O or event it waited for is complete
questions.explain: Only the scheduler moves a process into the running state, and a process that was waiting always passes through ready first.

questions.prompt: A process that was waiting for disk I/O sees its I/O finish. Which state does it enter?
questions.explain: It becomes ready and has to wait for the scheduler to give it the CPU again.

questions.prompt: Which statements are true about two processes started from the same program?
questions.explain: Two instances of a program do not share variables. Each one is a separate process with its own identifier and its own control block.
option_notes: False: each has its own copy of the data. Sharing needs an explicit mechanism.

questions.prompt: How are the processes of a Unix system related to each other?
options: They are all independent: none creates another
They form a tree: every process was created by a parent
They are in a single list ordered by pid
questions.explain: Each process is created by another, its parent, so the system forms a tree whose root is the first process (`init`).

questions.prompt: Does the mechanism mainly move DATA between processes or only tell about an EVENT?
questions.explain: Pipes, shared memory and messages transfer data. Signals and semaphores only tell a process that something happened (or make it wait for that).

questions.prompt: Which IPC style lets processes on DIFFERENT machines communicate without sharing memory?
questions.explain: Message passing uses `send` and `receive`; the system hides where the other side is, so it also works over a network.

questions.prompt: With shared memory between two processes, who is responsible for the format of the data and for synchronising the accesses?
questions.explain: After the kernel maps the segment into both address spaces it does not intervene any more: the processes agree on the layout and must use semaphores or mutexes to avoid races.

questions.prompt: In message passing, a blocking `receive` makes the receiver {{0}} until a message is available (wait or continue?).
questions.explain: Blocking (synchronous) receive waits for a message. A non-blocking receive returns at once, with a message or an empty answer.

questions.prompt: With a blocking (synchronous) `send`, when does the sender continue?
options: When the receiver has received the message
questions.explain: A blocking send waits until the message has been received. A non-blocking send continues right away.

questions.prompt: Which of the three schedulers decides, very often, which ready process runs next?
questions.explain: The short-term (CPU) scheduler runs all the time, so it must be fast. The long-term one admits new processes and the medium-term one suspends and resumes processes.

questions.prompt: Which are advantages of threads over separate processes?
options: They share data without any special IPC
An error in one thread cannot damage the others
They can run in parallel on several CPUs
questions.explain: Threads share memory, so they are cheap and communicate easily, and they can use several CPUs. The price is that they also share every bug.
option_notes: False: they share memory, so one thread can corrupt data that another uses.

questions.prompt: During a context switch, where does the system save the state of the process that leaves the CPU?
options: In the file it was started from
questions.explain: The state and registers go into the PCB of the old process and the state of the new one is loaded from its PCB. The CPU does no useful work during the switch.
